findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: Formatting `owner_id` directly into the SQL statement via an f-string makes the database query vulnerable to SQL injection. Pass `owner_id` as a query parameter to `cursor.execute` instead of interpolating it into the query string.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker providing a crafted `owner_id` payload (e.g., `' OR '1'='1`) can alter query structure to view or modify unauthorized order records.
findings.title: Parameterize query to prevent SQL injection

findings.body: The loop starts at index 1 instead of 0, skipping the first element in `entries` when computing scores and ranking.
findings.failure_scenario: When `rank_invoice_entries` is called with entries, the entry at index 0 is ignored and omitted from the returned list.
findings.title: Iterate over all entries starting from index 0

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: Using `events: list[str] = []` defines a mutable default argument that persists and accumulates appended items across subsequent function calls.
findings.failure_scenario: Successive invocations of `register_shipment_events` without passing an explicit `events` list will append to the same shared list, leaking event entries across unrelated calls.
findings.title: Avoid mutable default argument for `events`

findings.body: `flag_large_backorder_totals` takes a `threshold` parameter but checks against a hardcoded constant `5000` instead.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling `flag_large_backorder_totals` with a custom `threshold` (e.g. 1000) evaluates against 5000, incorrectly omitting rows that exceed the requested threshold.
findings.title: Compare backorder total against `threshold`

findings.body: `datetime.datetime.utcnow()` is deprecated since Python 3.12. Use `datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)` to generate an explicit, timezone-aware UTC datetime.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling `datetime.datetime.utcnow()` emits a `DeprecationWarning` in Python 3.12+ and produces a naive datetime lacking timezone information, causing failures or subtle offsets when interacting with timezone-aware systems.
findings.title: Replace deprecated datetime.utcnow() with timezone-aware datetime.now()

findings.anchor: """Return the newest queue identifier in constant time.
findings.body: The docstring states that the identifier is returned in constant time assuming records arrive in chronological order, but the implementation sorts the entire `records` list by `created_at`.
findings.title: Update docstring to reflect that newest_queue_id sorts the records

findings.body: Checking membership in a `list` with `if label in seen:` performs an O(n) linear scan on each iteration, causing `unique_payment_labels` to run in O(n²) time. Maintaining a separate `set` alongside `labels` allows O(1) membership lookups.
findings.failure_scenario: When `rows` contains many entries, repeatedly scanning `seen` as a list degrades performance quadratically and increases execution time.
findings.title: Use a set for membership checks to avoid quadratic lookup time

findings.body: The nested loops over `zones` and `weights` do not depend on `carrier` and compute the identical `count` for every iteration. Calculating `count` once before the `for carrier in carriers:` loop eliminates redundant O(|carriers| * |zones| * |weights|) work.
findings.failure_scenario: When `carriers`, `zones`, and `weights` lists are large, re-computing the same zone and weight pairings for each carrier causes unnecessary CPU utilization and latency.
findings.title: Hoist the viable route combination calculation out of the carrier loop

findings.body: The inner loops evaluate zone and weight combinations independently of the carrier, causing identical computations to be repeated across every carrier in an $O(|carriers| \times |zones| \times |weights|)$ triply nested structure. Calculating the valid count once flattens the function and avoids redundant iterations.
findings.suggestion:
viable_count = sum(1 for zone in zones if zone for weight in weights if weight > 0)
    return {carrier: viable_count for carrier in carriers}
findings.title: Compute route count outside the carrier loop to eliminate nested loops

findings.body: Maintaining separate `seen` and `labels` lists with linear membership checks manually reinvents ordered deduplication. In Python 3.7+, `dict.fromkeys()` preserves insertion order and collapses this loop into a single expression.
findings.title: Deduplicate labels with dict.fromkeys()

findings.body: Formatting `owner_id` directly into the SQL query string creates a SQL injection vulnerability when `owner_id` contains untrusted user input. Use query parameters passed directly to `cursor.execute()` rather than string interpolation.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplying a malicious payload (such as `' OR '1'='1`) as `owner_id` can bypass query filtering or execute arbitrary SQL statements to exfiltrate or modify order data.
findings.title: Parameterize SQL query to prevent SQL injection

findings.body: `datetime.datetime.utcnow()` is deprecated starting in Python 3.12 and returns a naive datetime object lacking explicit timezone information.
findings.failure_scenario: Running on Python 3.12+ raises a DeprecationWarning, and producing naive timestamps risks incorrect time conversions or comparison errors with timezone-aware datetime consumers.
findings.title: Replace deprecated `datetime.utcnow()` with timezone-aware `now()`

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: Using a mutable list as a default parameter causes `events` to be shared and retained across invocations. Over time, every call that relies on the default argument appends to this persistent list, resulting in unbounded memory growth and increasingly expensive `list(events)` copies.
findings.failure_scenario: Repeated calls to `register_shipment_events` without passing an `events` argument will accumulate events across all invocations into the shared list, resulting in unbounded memory growth and degraded response times when copying the list.
findings.title: Avoid mutable default argument to prevent unbounded list growth

findings.anchor: """Return the newest queue identifier in constant time.
findings.body: The docstring states that the function operates in constant time by assuming records arrive in chronological order, but the implementation explicitly sorts the entire list by `created_at`, running in O(n log n) time.
findings.title: Update docstring to reflect sorting behavior and complexity

findings.body: Checking membership with `if label in seen:` against a list requires an O(n) linear scan on each iteration. For large input sizes, this makes deduplication run in O(n²) time instead of linear time with a set.
findings.failure_scenario: When `rows` contains tens of thousands of items, checking membership against `seen: list[str]` performs an O(n) search per row, causing quadratic CPU time and degrading pipeline throughput.
findings.title: Use a set for deduplication lookups to avoid O(n²) scaling

findings.body: The inner loops over `zones` and `weights` do not depend on `carrier`, so re-evaluating them inside the carrier loop adds unnecessary triply-nested iteration. Precomputing the count once simplifies the logic and avoids redundant work per carrier.
findings.title: Calculate viable combinations outside the carrier loop

findings.body: `seen` and `labels` maintain the exact same elements in parallel. Using a `set` for membership checks or `dict.fromkeys` preserves first-seen order while removing duplicate state management and eliminating linear scans over `seen`.
findings.title: Eliminate redundant duplicate list tracking

findings.body: Building a separate list of (score, entry) tuples and unwrapping them after sorting replicates what sorted() already handles with a key function. Passing the slice directly to sorted() eliminates the loop and temporary list.
findings.title: Simplify ranking logic using sorted() with key

findings.body: `datetime.datetime.utcnow()` is deprecated since Python 3.12 and returns a naive datetime without timezone information. Replace it with `datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)`.
findings.failure_scenario: In Python 3.12+, calling `utcnow()` emits a `DeprecationWarning` and produces a naive timestamp that causes a `TypeError` if compared against timezone-aware datetime objects.
findings.title: Use timezone-aware datetime.now()

findings.anchor: """Return the newest queue identifier in constant time.
findings.body: The docstring claims the function operates in constant time and assumes records are already provided in chronological order. However, the implementation sorts the entire collection on `created_at`, running in O(N log N) time regardless of input ordering.
findings.suggestion: """Return the identifier of the newest record by created_at."""
findings.title: Correct docstring complexity and ordering assumptions in newest_queue_id

findings.body: Checking membership in a list (`seen`) performs an O(N) scan for each entry, making deduplication across `rows` run in O(N²) time instead of linear O(N) time with a set.
findings.failure_scenario: When `rows` contains a large number of payment records, the linear lookup in `seen` causes quadratic execution time, leading to high CPU usage and request latency.
findings.title: Use a set for deduplication tracking

findings.body: The inner nested loops iterate over all `zones` and `weights` to compute `count`, but this value is identical for every carrier. Recalculating it inside the `for carrier in carriers:` loop multiplies the work by the number of carriers unnecessarily.
findings.failure_scenario: When processing lists of carriers, zones, and weights, the function redundantly re-evaluates the nested zone and weight loops for every carrier, causing O(carriers × zones × weights) runtime instead of O(zones × weights + carriers).
findings.title: Hoist the tariff route count computation outside the carrier loop

findings.body: The inner loops iterating over `zones` and `weights` do not depend on `carrier`. Re-evaluating them inside the carrier loop introduces unnecessary 3-level nesting and recalculates the exact same count for each carrier.
findings.suggestion:
count = sum(1 for zone in zones if zone for weight in weights if weight > 0)
    return {carrier: count for carrier in carriers}
findings.title: Compute the route combination count outside the carrier loop

findings.body: `seen` and `labels` maintain identical lists of strings, leading to redundant state and linear membership lookups (`label in seen`) on every iteration. Using a `set` for lookup simplifies the tracking logic and avoids quadratic search complexity.
findings.suggestion:
seen: set[str] = set()
    labels: list[str] = []
    for row in rows:
        label = str(row.get("label", ""))
        if label not in seen:
            seen.add(label)
            labels.append(label)
    return labels
findings.title: Use a set to track seen labels instead of duplicate list state

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: Formatting `owner_id` directly into the SQL statement via an f-string introduces a SQL injection vulnerability if untrusted input is passed to `load_order_rows`.
findings.failure_scenario: An unescaped or malicious `owner_id` value (e.g. `' OR '1'='1`) is passed to `load_order_rows`, executing arbitrary SQL against the database.
findings.title: Use parameterized queries instead of string interpolation

findings.body: `flag_large_backorder_totals` accepts a `threshold` argument and claims in its docstring to filter rows exceeding that review threshold, but instead compares against a hardcoded constant `5000`.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes `flag_large_backorder_totals(rows, threshold=1000)` expecting items over 1000 to be flagged, but rows between 1000 and 5000 are omitted because the threshold argument is ignored.
findings.title: Compare row total against the threshold parameter

findings.body: The function manually constructs a list of tuples, sorts them, and unwraps the result. Using Python's built-in `sorted(..., key=...)` achieves the same result directly in a single statement.
findings.suggestion: return sorted(entries[1:], key=lambda entry: float(entry.get("score", 0)), reverse=True)
findings.title: Use sorted() with a key function instead of manual Schwartzian transform
